gadgets.versions: 7.0.0 (measured live; the library behaved correctly -- the gadget is how it was called)
gadgets.sink: JwtSecurityTokenHandler.ReadToken used to fetch the claims the application acts on, while ValidateToken is called only for its return value
gadgets.payload: a token the handler can PARSE but not verify: header {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}, any payload, and an empty signature segment (note the trailing dot)
gadgets.effect: every claim is attacker-chosen. ReadToken parses without a key, so whatever ValidateToken concluded is irrelevant to the claims that are then used.
gadgets.precondition: the calling code must fail to stop on a validation failure. In ASP.NET Core that is usually a middleware that calls context.Response.Redirect(...) without `return` and still awaits _next(context): the response carries a 302 while the controller runs and renders anyway.
gadgets.trap: ValidateToken here returned bool.ToString(), which is "False" with a capital F, and the caller compared it to the literal "false" -- so the failure branch was unreachable even before the missing return. Check the CASE of any stringly-typed validation result. A browser follows the 302 and hides the whole thing, so probe with a client that does not follow redirects and read the body returned WITH the 302. Always run the three-way control (no cookie / garbage cookie / forged token) before calling a 200 a bypass.
